title: Verbal-fluency style score is reified as IQ with no criterion validation
claim: The VFS is a hand-weighted composite of surface text statistics. It is mapped to an IQ band by a hand-written table, then reported as a point IQ with a '95% CI' and classification. No criterion study (correlation with WAIS/Raven, norm sample) exists in the repo. Construct validity of 'text style = general intelligence' is assumed, not shown.

evidence.excerpt: The 95% CI is mathematically derived from the confidence tier, not from validation against a reference population.

impact_on_screened_person: A candidate is assigned a numeric IQ and a label such as 'Low' or 'Gifted' by an instrument whose only validity evidence is the author's thresholds; a hiring or admissions reader will treat this as a measurement.
fix: Refuse to emit IQ/classification as a measurement. Output only a labelled 'writing-style index' with explicit 'not an intelligence measure' text in every output format, and gate IQ fields behind a documented validation-study pass flag (default off).

title: No criterion validation: hand-set norms, weights and bands make the IQ mapping circular
claim: iq_norms.json, edu_norms.json and the VFS weights (0.35/0.25/0.25/0.15 plus every sub-weight and min-max range) are hand-set with no source, sample, N or citation. The VFS-to-IQ table is then the only thing that defines IQ, so outputs cannot be wrong by construction; golden fixtures only freeze the tool's own outputs. No correlation with a standardised IQ measure, reliability estimate or PPV/NPV at any cut-off and base rate exists, yet the outputs are used as screening classifications.

evidence.excerpt: absence: no source, sample, N, or citation field anywhere in iq_norms.json; only vfs_min/vfs_max/iq_min/iq_max/label/percentile_min
Verbal fluency — the richness, complexity, and coherence of written language — correlates with cognitive ability measures.

impact_on_screened_person: People are labelled 'Below Average' or 'Low' (IQ 55-89) and assigned an education level by constants nobody can defend, with no accountable basis for appeal.
fix: Write a validation-study protocol (criterion measure, per-language sample sizes, held-out evaluation, reliability, correlation/SEE, PPV/NPV at stated base rates, subgroup error reporting); until results exist, label IQ/percentile/education 'experimental, unvalidated'.
acceptance_test: doc: docs/validation/validation-protocol.md exists and names criterion measure, sample size, subgroup analyses and acceptance r/SEE thresholds

title: '95% CI' is a word-count heuristic, not measurement error, and is narrower than the tool's own stated error
claim: ci_half = round(15 - confidence*10) is a linear function of a word-count tier (+/-12 at <30 words, +/-6 at >=300). It is not derived from a standard error, test-retest reliability or validation against a criterion IQ, ignores language/register uncertainty, and contradicts the report's own '+/-10-15 pt error margin' line, yet it is printed as a '95% CI'. A text proxy with realistic validity (r~0.3-0.5) has a prediction interval of +/-25 points or more.

evidence.excerpt: **Error margins are real.** The 95% CI is mathematically derived from the confidence tier, not from validation against a reference population.
line("    • Text-based IQ estimation carries ±10–15 pt error margin")

impact_on_screened_person: A screened candidate is shown a narrow-looking interval (e.g. 103-115) that implies far more certainty than exists; a reviewer can treat a 109 vs 124 difference as meaningful and reject on it.
fix: Stop labelling the value a 95% CI. Until a validation study supplies an SEE, either withhold the interval or report a wide, explicitly 'uncalibrated heuristic range' (>= +/-25) and refuse IQ output for screening use.

title: Percentile is interpolated toward 95 inside every band: non-monotonic and contradicts the IQ
claim: percentile = band.percentile_min + position*(95 - band.percentile_min) interpolates every band toward a hard-coded 95. Verified: vfs 39.99 -> IQ 74 'Low' -> 95th percentile; vfs 54.99 -> IQ 89 -> 95; vfs 55 -> IQ 90 -> 25; vfs 69.99 -> IQ 109 -> 95. Percentile jumps 95 -> 25 across a 0.01 VFS change and is not derivable from the IQ via the normal CDF (IQ 109 is ~73rd).
impact_on_screened_person: Reports shown to hiring/admissions staff carry internally inconsistent figures (average IQ at 95th percentile) that either inflate or mislead; undermines any decision based on them.
fix: Compute percentile from the IQ point with the normal CDF (mean 100, SD 15) and drop the per-band interpolation; cap/mark extremes.

title: One English-derived VFS-to-IQ table is applied to both languages; lang is ignored in scoring
claim: compute_verbal_fluency_score receives lang but only echoes it; iq_norms.json has no per-language bands. Verified on parallel en/id translations of the same paragraph: English VFS 47.5 -> IQ 82 / D3, Indonesian VFS 61.8 -> IQ 99 / S1 (a ~17 point gap for identical content). Cross-language scores are not comparable, so mixed en/id applicant pools get systematically different outcomes.

evidence.excerpt: line("    • IQ/VFS norms are English-derived and only approximately adapted to")

impact_on_screened_person: Applicants writing in Indonesian are scored on a different effective scale than English writers and can be ranked above or below peers purely because of language, with no disclosure in --json/--scores-only output.
fix: Refuse or loudly flag any cross-language comparison; add per-language norm tables with documented calibration data, and until validated emit a language_norm_unvalidated flag in every output and block rank-ordering across languages.

title: Unsupported languages and code-switched text silently analysed as English
claim: detect_language forces any non-en/id result (Javanese, Sundanese, Malay-mixed, etc.) to en at 0.50 confidence, and the pipeline never gates on that confidence. Verified: a Javanese paragraph returns lang=en conf=0.5; an en/id code-switched sentence returns en. Javanese-influenced or code-switching writers are scored with English tokenisation, readability and norms.
impact_on_screened_person: A candidate who writes in regional language, or mixes languages naturally, receives an IQ/education estimate that is meaningless but presented as normal output.
fix: Return an explicit unsupported_language / mixed_language status with no IQ, mental age or education output when detection confidence is below a threshold or the language is not en/id; add segment-level language ID for code-switching.

title: Punctuation alone swings IQ ~35 points: unpunctuated chat text collapses into one giant sentence
claim: For Indonesian the sentencizer splits only on punctuation and readability splits on '.', so unpunctuated chat/transcript text (which README invites) becomes one sentence and mean sentence length, Fog and ARI explode. Verified with run_pipeline on the same 35-word Indonesian chat message: unpunctuated -> VFS 73.3, IQ 113, edu S2; with three full stops added -> VFS 43.7, IQ 78, edu SD. Sentence-length scores measure typing habits, not syntactic ability.

evidence.excerpt: Works on any text type: essays, social media posts, chat logs, transcripts.

impact_on_screened_person: A candidate who writes chat-style without full stops can be scored ~35 IQ points and four education levels higher (or lower) than the same words punctuated.
fix: Detect low-punctuation input (words per terminal mark above a threshold) and refuse sentence-length-based metrics or route to INSUFFICIENT_STRUCTURE; cap per-sentence length used in MSL/readability; document that punctuation density is a confound.

title: Genre, register, topic, editing and L1 confounds are uncontrolled: style proxy presented as IQ
claim: The pipeline infers a person's IQ from group-level correlations between text complexity and cognition. Sentence length, rare words, subordination and readability indices are dominated by education, genre (chat vs essay), editing, topic and first language. README advertises use on 'chat logs, transcripts' and social posts with no genre control; mental age and education are derived from the same signal, so they are not independent. No covariate adjustment is applied.

evidence.excerpt: Predict IQ, mental age, and education level from text passages using verbal fluency as a psycholinguistic proxy. Supports **English** and **Indonesian**. Works on any text type: essays, social media posts, chat logs, transcripts.
Verbal fluency — the richness, complexity, and coherence of written language — correlates with cognitive ability measures.

impact_on_screened_person: Second-language writers, people with less formal schooling, or someone who wrote casual chat text are scored as lower-intelligence; the tool encodes class and language background as 'IQ'.
fix: Refuse or heavily degrade IQ output unless text type is declared as formal prose of a minimum length; report 'writing-style complexity' instead of IQ; add genre/L1 warnings and a no-individual-decision notice.

title: Short-text scores are still emitted as a point IQ with a narrow-looking CI
claim: Confidence is a pure word-count lookup (<30 words = 0.30, VERY LOW), but predict_iq still returns a point estimate and a +/-12 CI for 10-30 word inputs. MATTR falls back to plain TTR below 50 tokens and hapax_ratio (weighted 0.30 of lexical) is strongly length-dependent: a 12-token sentence gives hapax_ratio 0.90, i.e. a very high lexical score. vocd is skipped under 50 tokens. Small-sample metrics are length-biased and extremely noisy.

evidence.excerpt: return len(set(tokens)) / len(tokens) if tokens else 0.0
hapax_ratio = round(hapax_count / len(freq), 3) if freq else 0.0

impact_on_screened_person: A candidate who submits a short statement gets a numeric IQ that is mostly a length artefact; a short text can score higher on lexical diversity than a long, rich one.
fix: Return status INSUFFICIENT_TEXT with no IQ, percentile or education output below a configurable minimum word count (e.g. 250); use length-robust metrics (MTLD/HD-D) and drop raw hapax ratio.

title: Indonesian passive detection is a prefix regex with a hand-written denylist; non-passives counted as passive
claim: _ID_PASSIVE_RE matches any di-/ter- word of 4+ letters. Verified: 'terjadi', 'terkait', 'terbaik', 'dimana', 'diantara' are counted as passive (passive_ratio 1.0 for 'Hal itu terjadi dan terkait dengan hasil terbaik dimana kami berada diantara mereka'). The denylist is a finite hand-curated list that cannot enumerate Indonesian morphology. The metric feeds the evidence and report, with no measured precision.
impact_on_screened_person: Indonesian writers get structurally different, partly spurious syntactic features than English writers, so cross-language scores are not comparable.
fix: Replace denylist with an allowlist/verb lexicon or morphological analyser (e.g. di- + known verb stem via Sastrawi); measure precision on a labelled sample.

title: Indonesian clause density counts noun coordination and temporal prepositions as clauses
claim: clause_counts = 1 + subs + coords, where coords includes 'dan','atau','serta' (also NP/word-level coordinators) and subs includes prepositions like sejak/selama/sampai/sebelum/setelah/hingga. Verified: 'Saya makan nasi dan atau minum teh sejak pagi sampai malam selama seminggu' (one clause) yields clause_density 6.0 and subordination_index 3.0, scoring 74.2. clause_density is 35% of syntactic score, so one frequent coordinator inflates the score and stacking prepositions rewards padding.

evidence.excerpt: gunning_fog: float, ari: float, lexical_density: float, clause_density: float

impact_on_screened_person: Indonesian texts are scored higher or lower on syntax for lexical-list reasons, not structure; the same ability yields different scores in English vs Indonesian.
fix: Count clause joiners only where they link verbal clauses (require a verb/predicate on both sides) and split the prepositional senses out of ID_SUBORDINATORS.

title: Semantic entity score uses English NER labels but Indonesian model emits PER/ORG/LOC/MISC; 'person' scores lowest
claim: ABSTRACT_TYPES/CONCRETE_TYPES are English OntoNotes labels (LAW, NORP, PERSON, GPE...). xx_ent_wiki_sm only emits LOC, MISC, ORG, PER (verified via ner.labels). For Indonesian text, mentioning an ORG gives ABSTRACT (80), LOC gives CONCRETE (50), and PER/MISC or nothing gives MINIMAL (20). Mentioning a company is treated as more 'sophisticated' than mentioning a person, in both languages; named-entity presence is not a measure of intellect.
impact_on_screened_person: Topic choice (talking about people vs organisations) moves a person's score by up to 6 points of semantic score, penalising subjects who write about individuals.
fix: Remove entity_sophistication from the score (or ground it in a validated measure); at minimum map labels per model and do not weight it.

title: Indonesian readability and education use English-calibrated Fog/ARI/Coleman-Liau and Flesch coefficients
claim: readability.py always calls textstat.set_lang('en_US') and computes Gunning Fog, ARI and Coleman-Liau with English syllable/letter rules even for lang == 'id'; only Flesch is customised, using English coefficients (206.835/1.015/84.6). edu_norms.json then maps these US-grade-calibrated values straight to Indonesian levels (SMP/SMA/S1/S2/S3). The thresholds are uncalibrated for Indonesian orthography and there is no Indonesian schooling norm.

evidence.excerpt: content_words = [t for t in alpha if len(t) > 3]

impact_on_screened_person: An Indonesian applicant can be graded as SD/SMP vs S2 by an English formula's artefacts (verified: a simple 3-sentence Indonesian text yields Fog 4.8), with consequences for admissions placement.
fix: Do not emit an education level for lang == 'id' until Indonesian-calibrated readability and norms exist; return 'not available' with reason.

title: Education matching uses a brittle AND of three uncalibrated cutoffs with a meaningless confidence
claim: A level is matched only when fog, ari AND lexical_density all clear the thresholds, so one low metric drops the person to a lower level (verified: fog=20, ari=2, density 0.7 -> 'Primary School' with confidence 0.82 HIGH). The 'confidence' counts margins above the matched level's own thresholds (+1,+1,+0.05), so the floor level SD has all-zero minima and always scores HIGH. clause_density is a parameter but is never used.

evidence.excerpt: gunning_fog: float, ari: float, lexical_density: float, clause_density: float

impact_on_screened_person: A single noisy index (e.g. ARI on short sentences) can drop an applicant several education levels while the output claims HIGH confidence.
fix: Use a continuous composite or modal score with an uncertainty range, drop the margin-based confidence, and remove or use clause_density.

title: 'lexical_density' is a word-length proxy (len>3) that favours Indonesian affixation and is double-counted
claim: lexical_density is defined as the share of tokens longer than 3 characters, not content-word ratio. It correlates with avg_word_length (also scored, 0.15) so word length is counted twice in the lexical score, and the same value is an education gate in edu_norms.json. Verified: 'the cat sat on the mat and the dog ran to the park' gives density 0.077. Indonesian function words (yang, dari, untuk, dengan, adalah) are >3 letters and count as 'content'.

evidence.excerpt: content_words = [t for t in alpha if len(t) > 3]

impact_on_screened_person: Indonesian text (long function words, agglutinative morphology) scores systematically higher/lower on a length artefact, shifting both IQ and education.
fix: Compute content-word ratio via POS tags or stop-word lists per language; remove one of the collinear length metrics.

title: Unmeasurable components are imputed as numbers (semantic 50.0, lexical 0.0) and blended into VFS at full weight
claim: When a text has <2 sentences (or no within-document transitions) analyze_semantic returns score 50.0 with coherence None, and compute_verbal_fluency_score still weights it at 0.25. Missing data is imputed as an average ability, pulling short or single-sentence submissions toward the middle (regression to the mean made to look like a measurement). The syntactic ID path does the honest thing (drops and renormalises); semantic does not.
impact_on_screened_person: A candidate with a single long paragraph (one sentence per tokenizer) receives a mid-range semantic score regardless of real coherence, biasing the final IQ towards 'Average'.
fix: Return score None and renormalise the weights in compute_verbal_fluency_score when a component is unavailable; surface it in the report.

title: Ratio mental age (IQ/100 x age) is applied to adults with an assumed age of 30
claim: predict_mental_age applies the ratio-IQ mental age model to any chronological age and defaults to 30 when age is unknown. The ratio model is invalid beyond adolescence (verified: IQ 120 at age 70 gives mental age 84; IQ 100 at 8 gives 8). It is also dependent on the unvalidated IQ point, so any error is multiplied by age. The reported figure is not a psychometric quantity.

evidence.excerpt: Compute mental age from IQ. Pass chronological_age=0 to use population default (30).

impact_on_screened_person: A mature applicant with a mid-range score is told their 'mental age' is e.g. 84 or 27, which reads as a cognitive deficit and is meaningless.
fix: Drop mental age for age > 16 and when age is assumed; otherwise withhold the number and explain why.

title: Indonesian syntactic lexicon is formal-register only; colloquial and dialect writing is penalised
claim: ID_SUBORDINATORS/ID_CLAUSE_COORDINATORS contain only standard-register conjunctions. Colloquial and Javanese-influenced forms (kalo, biar, soalnya, makanya, pas, gara-gara, nek, ben) are absent, so informal but fully complex sentences receive lower subordination and clause density; the passive detector also only knows di-/ter- morphology.
impact_on_screened_person: Candidates who write in everyday or regionally-influenced Indonesian are scored lower than those using formal register, a proxy for region and class rather than ability.
fix: Normalise colloquial/dialect variants to standard forms (or extend the lexicon with register-tagged entries) before counting, and add register-parity tests; report detected register as a limiting factor.

title: Education level is inferred from readability and treated as formal schooling attainment
claim: estimate_education_level maps Fog/ARI/lexical density thresholds directly to degree levels (S3...SD). Readability measures text difficulty, which depends on topic, audience and editing; it is not a function of the writer's schooling. The level labels are hand-set and unvalidated. Verified: a plain-language English passage returns edu 'SD' (Primary School) and IQ 66.

evidence.excerpt: line(f"  Writing style consistent with {edu_result['level_en']} authorship.")

impact_on_screened_person: A person who writes plainly (professional plain-language training, ESL, a different register) is labelled primary-school educated; a ghostwritten or template-heavy text is labelled doctoral. Education claims could be used to reject or approve people on a false basis.
fix: Rename to 'text complexity band' with no degree labels; never output S1/S2/S3/SD codes as the writer's education. Add explicit warning that education cannot be inferred from text.

title: No control for AI-assisted writing, translation, dictation or ghostwriting
claim: Authorship provenance is never checked or asked. LLM-polished, machine-translated, dictated or edited text raises lexical and syntactic scores while the pipeline reports the result as the person's own verbal ability. The report asserts 'authorship' directly. No provenance field exists in any tool signature.

evidence.excerpt: line(f"  Writing style consistent with {edu_result['level_en']} authorship.")
absence: no tool takes an authorship/provenance/assistance parameter and no output carries one

impact_on_screened_person: A candidate who wrote unaided is outscored by one who used an LLM or editor, and a candidate who wrote through a screen reader or dictation is penalised; the result is attributed to the person as their own.
fix: Add mandatory provenance attestation in the input schema, print it on every report, and label scores 'valid only for supervised, unaided, same-prompt writing'; refuse hiring-use output without it.

title: Hapax and MATTR components bias scores by text length and then confidence rewards length
claim: Hapax ratio is a monotone-decreasing function of text length (Heaps law) and is weighted 30% of the lexical score with fixed [0.2,0.7] scaling; MATTR is window-fixed but avg word length and ratios are not length-normalised. Long texts are scored on a different effective scale than short ones, and confidence rises with length at the same time. Verified on one passage: 117 words -> VFS 55.2, 861 words -> 61.9.

evidence.excerpt: hapax_ratio = round(hapax_count / len(freq), 3) if freq else 0.0

impact_on_screened_person: The same writer gets different IQ values depending on how much they were asked to write; a short test sample can systematically push a person down a band.
fix: Replace raw hapax ratio with a length-corrected measure (e.g. fixed-window hapax or MTLD), calibrate with samples truncated to fixed lengths, and add a length-invariance test.

title: Readability and syntactic components re-measure word and sentence length, so nominal VFS weights are misleading
claim: Across components (not within lexical, see the lexical_density finding), the readability sub-score is built from Fog, ARI and Coleman-Liau, which are functions of words-per-sentence and syllables/characters-per-word, while the syntactic sub-score's largest-but-one input is mean sentence length. Readability (0.15) and syntactic (0.25) therefore re-measure the same two length statistics that lexical already uses, so the nominal 0.35/0.25/0.25/0.15 split does not describe what actually drives the VFS. No component correlation matrix or effective-weight analysis exists.
impact_on_screened_person: People who write long sentences or long words are rewarded in several components for one surface trait, inflating or deflating their IQ estimate.
fix: Compute the cross-component correlation matrix on a reference corpus, publish effective weights, and remove or orthogonalise redundant length-driven components before re-weighting.

title: English and Indonesian syntactic scores come from different instruments placed on the same curves
claim: English clause/subordination counts come from spaCy dependency labels, Indonesian counts from a conjunction word list, and Indonesian drops dependency depth and renormalises the remaining weights by 0.90; both are then mapped through identical min-max curves on the claim that this keeps scales comparable. No equating study shows a given Indonesian clause_density means the same as the English one.

evidence.excerpt: # Reuse the SAME component-scoring curves as English so scales stay comparable.
clauses = sum(1 for t in doc if t.dep_ in CLAUSE_DEPS)

impact_on_screened_person: Indonesian and English writers with the same syntactic skill receive systematically different syntactic scores, feeding 25% of VFS.
fix: Run a parallel-text equating study (en/id translations) for each syntactic component, publish the per-language curves, and flag id syntactic scores as non-comparable until done.

title: Misspellings and orthographic variation are scored as lexical sophistication
claim: MATTR, hapax ratio and evidence 'rare words' count every distinct token with no spelling normalisation; a paragraph with deliberate typos scored higher than the clean version (VFS 48.4 vs 47.5). Spelling errors from dyslexia, non-native writing or keyboard noise therefore raise diversity metrics, and there is no accommodation mode or disability disclosure path.

evidence.excerpt: hapax_count = sum(1 for f in freq.values() if f == 1)
hapax_ratio = round(hapax_count / len(freq), 3) if freq else 0.0
rare = [w for w in words if freq.get(w.lower(), 0) == 1 and len(w) > 5]

impact_on_screened_person: Scores track error rate and noise rather than skill, so dyslexic or non-native applicants get unpredictable results, and nothing tells the reviewer that an accommodation or alternative assessment may be needed.
fix: Spell-normalise tokens before diversity metrics and flag high-misspelling texts as low reliability routed to human review.

title: Dominance of surface complexity: the VFS cannot distinguish ornate from competent
claim: Every sub-score rewards longer words, longer sentences, rarer tokens and more subordination (monotone increasing). There is no check for correctness, relevance, argument quality or fluency errors; padding with jargon raises the score. 'Verbal fluency' (generation rate) is also a different construct from this readability-style index but shares the name.

evidence.excerpt: Predict IQ, mental age, and education level from text passages using verbal fluency as a psycholinguistic proxy.

impact_on_screened_person: A candidate who communicates clearly and concisely (usually what employers need) is scored lower than one who pads text, rewarding obfuscation.
fix: Rename the construct 'lexical-syntactic complexity', document that it rewards complexity not quality, and add an adversarial-padding test that the system flags rather than rewards.

title: Research-basis block implies validation the cited works do not provide
claim: The report ends with a RESEARCH BASIS list (Pennebaker, Crossley, Mairesse) printed on every full report, implying the mapping reproduces those studies. Those studies report modest correlations at group level with personality or essay quality, not individual IQ estimation, and nothing in the repo reproduces their coefficients.

evidence.excerpt: line("  Pennebaker et al.   — LIWC personality/intelligence studies")
line("  Mairesse et al.     — Big Five + intelligence from text")

impact_on_screened_person: Authority-by-citation lends false scientific weight to a decision about a person and discourages reviewers from questioning the score.
fix: Replace 'Research basis' with 'Inspired by' and add the real effect sizes / 'no individual-level validation' sentence; remove names from the report unless a reproduction is documented.

title: Population-level norm presented as individual causal claim; mean-age default hides age effect
claim: Verbal style changes with age, schooling era, dialect and disability, none of which enter predict_iq; chronological age is only used for the mental-age ratio. The default of 30 is called 'population median', not a validated one. No age-norming exists, so older or younger writers are compared against an unspecified reference.

evidence.excerpt: `default_chronological_age` is used when no `--age=N` flag is supplied. Set to the population median (30).

impact_on_screened_person: Age, dyslexia, second-language status and education era shift scores independent of ability; the person is nonetheless ranked against an anonymous reference.
fix: Define the reference population and norm groups in a written norming plan; require age and language-background fields and report within-group scores only.
acceptance_test: doc: docs/validation/norming-plan.md exists and defines reference population, age bands and language-background strata

title: Two-sentence texts get a perfect topic-drift score because the std of one value is zero
claim: topic_drift_index is the standard deviation of adjacent-sentence similarities; with exactly two sentences there is one value, so std = 0.0 and drift_score = 100 (verified: a two-sentence en text with an unrelated second sentence returns topic_drift_index 0.0). Drift is 25% of the semantic score, so the shortest texts receive the best 'focus' rating.
impact_on_screened_person: Very short submissions are credited with maximal topical focus they never demonstrated.
fix: Require a minimum number of transitions (e.g. >= 5) for drift; otherwise return None and renormalise.

title: Indonesian MATTR uses stems while hapax uses surface forms and English uses neither
claim: For lang='id' MATTR is computed on Sastrawi stems (collapsing affixed variants) but the hapax ratio on lowercased surface forms; English gets no lemmatisation for either. The two diversity components therefore measure different units per language and pull in opposite directions for Indonesian (stemming lowers MATTR, affixation raises hapax).
impact_on_screened_person: Lexical scores of Indonesian and English writers are not on a common unit.
fix: Use the same unit (lemma) for all diversity metrics in both languages and document it.

title: 'Argument coherence' is paraphrase similarity on uncalibrated 0.3-0.9 scaling shared by both languages
claim: argument_coherence is the mean cosine similarity of adjacent sentence embeddings from a paraphrase model, then linearly scaled from 0.3-0.9 for both languages. Paraphrase similarity measures lexical/semantic overlap, not argument structure, and multilingual embedding similarity baselines differ by language; the 0.3/0.6 constants are unsourced.
impact_on_screened_person: A well-argued text that moves between ideas scores lower than a repetitive one; scores shift by language for reasons unrelated to the writer.
fix: Rename to 'adjacent-sentence similarity', calibrate scaling per language on a reference corpus, and stop describing it as argument coherence in the report.

title: word_count counts numbers, emoji and symbols, so confidence tiers can be reached by non-words
claim: word_count counts every non-space, non-punctuation spaCy token, including numbers and symbols (verified: 'Total 12345 67890 2024 100 200 300 400 500 is fine.' -> word_count 11), while lexical metrics use only alphabetic tokens. Confidence and the CI width are set from this inflated count.

evidence.excerpt: word_count = len([t for t in doc if not t.is_space and not t.is_punct])

impact_on_screened_person: Number-heavy or emoji-heavy text receives a higher confidence label than its words justify.
fix: Base word_count (and confidence) on alphabetic word tokens, and report both counts.

title: Heuristic confidences are printed as percentages, implying calibrated probabilities
claim: The report prints 'Analysis confidence : HIGH (95%)', 'Lang detection conf : 73%' and education 'Confidence : HIGH (82%)'. These numbers are a word-count step function, a sigmoid of a log-prob margin divided by an arbitrary 30, and a count of margins over thresholds; none is a probability of being correct.
impact_on_screened_person: Reviewers read '95% confidence' as near-certainty about a person's score.
fix: Show ordinal labels only (or rename to 'heuristic index'); never format these values as percentages.

title: Band label strings use clinical psychometric terms ('Gifted / Highly Gifted', 'Low')
claim: Independently of whether an IQ figure is emitted at all (see the reified-IQ finding), the band label strings in iq_norms.json are clinical psychometric categories ('Gifted / Highly Gifted', 'Below Average', 'Low') and the reporter prints them under 'Classification'. Even if the output is relabelled a style index, these strings would still stigmatise a person.
impact_on_screened_person: A person is labelled 'Low' on the basis of writing style.
fix: Rename the band label strings in iq_norms.json to neutral style-band names (e.g. 'Style band 1-5') and change the reporter heading from 'Classification' to 'Style band'.

title: Vocabulary stuffing trivially inflates IQ estimate (no adversarial robustness)
claim: Scores reward rare/long words and long sentences with no gaming detection. Demonstrated with .venv/bin/python run_pipeline: a plain 36-word text scored VFS 29.3 / IQ 69 / edu SD; a 34-word text of stacked nominalisations ('Notwithstanding epistemological heterogeneity, the ontological ramifications...') scored VFS 61.7 / IQ 98 / edu S3 with no semantic content. A coached applicant can add ~30 IQ points; conversely honest plain writers are penalised.
impact_on_screened_person: Screened people who know the metric (or use an LLM to rewrite their text) outrank honest candidates; the decision rewards gaming, not ability.

title: Per-metric explanation of why a score came out as it did
claim: The report gives a composite VFS but no contribution breakdown tying weighted components to the final number or to what would change it.
impact_on_screened_person: A rejected candidate cannot learn which factor drove the outcome, and reviewers cannot challenge it.
fix: Add a 'contributions' block (weight x score per metric, rank, sensitivity) to compute_verbal_fluency_score and render it in the report.

title: Score appeal and contestation path
claim: There is no mechanism for a screened person to contest a score or request rescoring with human review.

evidence.excerpt: **Do not use for consequential decisions.** These estimates must not be used for hiring, clinical assessment, academic evaluation, or legal proceedings.
absence: no appeal, dispute or re-score API

impact_on_screened_person: A person harmed by a wrong score has no recourse, a legal exposure under automated-decision rules.
fix: Write an appeal procedure (intake, SLA, independent reviewer, rescoring with alternate text) and a tool recording appeal status.
acceptance_test: doc: docs/process/appeal-procedure.md exists and defines intake, SLA, independent reviewer and outcome records

title: AI-generated text detection flag
claim: Nothing flags text likely written by an LLM, whose fluency inflates VFS.

evidence.excerpt: absence: no AI-text or authorship-integrity signal

impact_on_screened_person: Candidates using LLMs get inflated scores over honest ones; or honest candidates are mis-judged.
fix: Add an advisory heuristic flag (low-perplexity/uniformity) with explicit false-positive warning; never auto-penalise.

title: API authentication for the MCP server
claim: The server exposes all tools with no authentication or caller identity; harmless over local stdio but required before any HTTP/shared deployment.
impact_on_screened_person: Anyone reaching the server can score people's text; no accountability trail for who ran what.
fix: Add token auth middleware for non-stdio transports and attach caller identity to every call.

title: Per-caller rate limiting and abuse throttling
claim: No limit on call rate per caller; one client can monopolise the single-process server.

evidence.excerpt: absence: no rate limit or max text length

impact_on_screened_person: Enables probing the scorer to gaming-optimise text and denial of service for other users.
fix: Add per-caller rate limit and max input size with explicit errors.

title: Batch scoring with per-document results and error isolation
claim: Only single-text scoring exists; reviewers must script loops and one bad input breaks the flow.
impact_on_screened_person: Manual loops invite inconsistent handling and copy-paste mistakes across candidates.
fix: Add tool_score_batch accepting a list of documents returning per-document result or structured error.

title: Writing-improvement feedback for the screened person
claim: Output is evaluative only; no actionable guidance for the author.
impact_on_screened_person: Candidates get a verdict but no path to improve, which reduces perceived fairness.
fix: Add 'suggestions' section from weakest metrics with sentence-level examples (repetition, long sentences).

title: Language expansion beyond English and Indonesian
claim: Only English and Indonesian are supported and there is no defined way to add a language with its own tokenisation, readability and norms.
impact_on_screened_person: Text in other languages is scored against English norms with no refusal.
fix: Define a language-pack interface (tokeniser, function words, readability, norms) and register en/id through it.

title: Multi-sample aggregation for the same person
claim: Each text is scored independently; no way to combine several samples to raise reliability.
impact_on_screened_person: Single-sample scores are noisy; one bad writing day determines the outcome.
fix: Add aggregate_samples(person_id, results) returning pooled VFS with narrower, honest CI and between-sample variance.

title: Structured machine-readable output schema with versioning
claim: Report JSON has no published schema, so integrators parse ad hoc.
impact_on_screened_person: Integrators mis-parse fields (e.g. N/A strings), causing wrong decisions downstream.
fix: Publish JSON Schema for the report and validate output against it in tests.

title: Confidence interval that reflects real measurement error
claim: CI width depends only on text-length tier, not per-metric variance or validation error.
impact_on_screened_person: Narrow CIs overstate precision for the person being judged.
fix: Compute CI from empirical residuals from the validation harness and bootstrapped metric variance.

title: Reviewer-facing evidence view with sentence citations
claim: Evidence is capped at three items per metric.
impact_on_screened_person: Reviewers cannot see why the score was reached beyond a few cherry-picked sentences.
fix: Add a verbose evidence mode returning all contributing sentences with their metric effect.

title: Accommodation mode for non-native writers and disabilities
claim: No option to adjust interpretation for ESL authors, dyslexia or assistive tools.
impact_on_screened_person: Protected groups get systematically lower scores without any adjustment path.
fix: Add accommodation flag that suppresses IQ/edu mapping and requires human review.

title: Single server-side scoring tool that runs the whole pipeline
claim: Scoring requires the agent to call 11 tools in order and pass JSON between them, which costs tokens, invites mistakes and lets the caller alter intermediate scores. scripts/pipeline.py already chains the steps but is not exposed as a tool.

evidence.excerpt: Call these tools in order. Each output feeds the next.

impact_on_screened_person: Scores cannot be altered between steps by the orchestrating agent.
fix: Add tool_score_text(text, options) that runs the full pipeline server-side and returns the report.

title: Standardised writing-task elicitation mode
claim: The tool scores any text type, so samples differ in genre, prompt, time and editing. There is no standard prompt set, time limit or 'unaided' attestation that would make samples comparable.

evidence.excerpt: Works on any text type: essays, social media posts, chat logs, transcripts.
Use this skill when the user provides one or more text passages from a

impact_on_screened_person: Everyone is assessed on the same task instead of on whatever text happened to be collected.
fix: Ship a prompt bank (en/id) with timing and length rules and record task_id on every scored sample.

title: Classification probabilities across bands instead of a single label
claim: predict_iq returns a single band label even when the estimate sits on a band edge, hiding that adjacent bands are almost equally likely.
impact_on_screened_person: A person near a boundary is not presented as definitively in the lower band.
fix: Return a probability for each band from the (validated) interval and show it in the report.

title: Non-prose content filter (lists, code, tables, quotations) before scoring
claim: Preprocessing strips only URLs, mentions and hashtags; bullet lists, code, tables and quoted material written by others are scored as the person's prose.
impact_on_screened_person: Quoted or pasted content does not inflate or deflate the person's score.
fix: Detect and exclude list/code/table/quotation blocks, report the excluded share, and lower confidence when high.

title: Offline model bundle for air-gapped installs
claim: The sentence-transformer is fetched from Hugging Face on first use, so a fully local install is not possible and the privacy statement depends on network state.

evidence.excerpt: No data is sent to external services beyond the embedding model (downloaded locally on first use).

impact_on_screened_person: Organisations can run scoring with no outbound network, keeping text on site.
fix: Provide a model bundle (pinned spaCy wheels + transformer snapshot) and an offline mode flag that refuses network fetches.

title: Candidate-facing plain-language score explanation in Bahasa Indonesia (UU PDP transparency)
claim: The only output is an English technical report written for an operator; there is no explanation addressed to the screened person, in their language, of what was measured, what it cannot tell about them and how to object. UU PDP 27/2022 gives data subjects a right to clear information about processing and profiling.
impact_on_screened_person: Indonesian candidates can understand, in plain Bahasa Indonesia, what was inferred about them and how to contest it.
fix: Add a subject_explanation output (id and en) in plain language: what was measured, its limits, that it is not an IQ test, and the contact/appeal route.

title: Split-half stability gate that withholds a score when two halves of the text disagree
claim: Nothing checks whether a submission scores consistently with itself: confidence is a word-count tier only. Scoring the first and second half of the same text separately would expose unstable results (mixed genres, pasted sections) before a single number is reported.
impact_on_screened_person: A person is not given a score that would change materially depending on which half of their own text was read.
fix: Add a stability check that scores two halves of the text (sentence-aligned), reports the VFS difference, and returns UNSTABLE with no IQ/education output above a threshold.

title: Data-subject access export of every score, label and evidence quote derived about a person
claim: There is no way to give a screened person a copy of everything derived about them (scores, labels, quoted evidence sentences, versions) as UU PDP right-of-access requires; outputs are returned once to the caller and not indexed by subject.

evidence.excerpt: absence: no subject_id on any tool and no access/export tool

impact_on_screened_person: A person can see exactly what was inferred about them and correct or contest it.
fix: Add subject_ref to scoring runs and an export tool that returns all derived records for a subject_ref.

title: Dry-run / what-if comparison between norm versions
claim: Cannot see how a candidate's score would change under revised norms.
impact_on_screened_person: Norm changes silently alter outcomes with no impact analysis.
fix: Add compare_norms(text, version_a, version_b) tool.

title: Sample-size advisor telling the submitter how much more text the refusal gate requires
claim: Confidence tiers are fixed word-count cut-offs (30/100/300) and the planned minimum-text refusal gate will reject short submissions, but the output never tells the person how many more words are needed to be scored at all or at the next tier.
impact_on_screened_person: A candidate who is refused can supply enough text to be assessed fairly instead of being dropped or scored on a fragment.
fix: Return words_needed_for_minimum and words_needed_for_next_tier in the VFS result and report.
